title:
Your 200-person biotech
already has *five*
AI use cases.
sub: Nobody approved them as a programme. Here is what each one actually needs.

title:
Ask your QA lead how many
AI use cases touch a
GxP decision today.
text:
The honest answer in most mid-size companies is "I would have to ask around."

That is not a governance failure. It is what happens when AI arrives as a feature rather than a project.

title:
Two questions decide
everything else.
text:
*How much does the AI influence the decision?*
Suggestion, draft, or the decision itself.

*What happens if it is wrong?*
Rework, a finding, or patient harm.
tag: Everything below is just these two applied

title:
Drafting SOPs,
protocols, reports.
text:
Influence: low. A human still authors and approves.
Consequence if wrong: rework, or a sloppy document nobody caught.

*Decision: proceed with controls.* The named author stays accountable. No AI text goes in without review, and the record shows AI was used.

title:
A chatbot answering
"what does our SOP say?"
text:
Influence: medium. People act on the answer without opening the document.
Consequence if wrong: someone follows a procedure that does not exist.

*Decision: proceed with controls.* Answers must cite the current effective document, and the bot must refuse when it has no source.

title:
Generating validation
test scripts.
text:
Influence: medium. The script decides what gets tested, and what does not.
Consequence if wrong: a gap in evidence that surfaces during an inspection, not before.

*Decision: proceed with controls.* A qualified reviewer approves coverage before execution. Speed is in the drafting, not the judgement.
tag: Review the coverage, not the grammar

title:
Flagging anomalies in
lab or process data.
text:
Influence: high. It shapes what a human investigates and what passes unexamined.
Consequence if wrong: a real signal is never looked at.

*Decision: validate.* Measure it against known cases, including the ones it should catch. Missing a true signal matters more than a false alarm.
tag: Here the misses are the risk

title:
The vendor feature that
arrived switched on.
text:
Influence: whatever the vendor decided.
Consequence if wrong: you own it, and you did not choose it.

*Decision: assess before the release goes live.* Read the release notes for AI features, decide on each, and record the decision. Default-on is still a decision, just not yours.
tag: Sachin Bhandari made this point well recently

title:
"Proceed with controls"
means five specific things:
items: *A named human* who owns the output, not the tool
*A grounded source* the answer can be traced back to
*A review step* where disagreeing is realistic, not theatre
*A recorded decision* saying why this level of control fits
*A trigger to revisit* when the model or the vendor changes

title:
And a short list where
no control is enough.
text:
AI signing a record. AI releasing product. AI closing a CAPA on its own. AI making a clinical decision. AI writing to a validated record with no human signature.

Those are refusals, not higher tiers. Knowing where your line sits is faster than debating each request.

title:
Has your org started the
AI-in-GxP journey?
text:
